changes.before: Explain what remains saved after stash apply, then optionally follow the complete disposable-repository companion. Do not use an active personal repository for practice.
changes.after: A stash can hold unfinished edits while you work on something else. Applying it keeps the saved stash.

before: Uncommitted tracked-file edits belong to the working tree. A stash can temporarily save those edits while you work on something else.

Use only a new empty disposable folder, with Git installed and configured. Create note.txt containing first. Then run git init, git add note.txt, and git commit -m "First note" in that folder. Change note.txt to draft and save without committing. Never run this practice inside an existing personal repository.

```bash
git status
git diff
git stash push -m "practice draft"
git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{0}
```
The tracked file returns to its committed content, while the stash keeps the saved difference. Inspect before relying on that result.

```bash
git stash apply stash@{0}
git diff
git stash list
```
apply restores the saved edits but keeps the stash entry. Confirm the file contains draft again and the entry remains listed.
pop tries to apply and, on success, remove the entry. Keeping apply and inspection separate is safer for this exercise; do not drop the stash until the recovered work is verified.
By default, ordinary stash push does not include untracked files. A new untracked file is not protected merely because tracked changes were stashed.
Applying onto conflicting edits can require conflict resolution. A stash is local working-change storage, not a remote backup or a published commit.
after: The working tree is the project files you can edit. A stash temporarily saves unfinished changes to tracked files: files Git already knows.

Use a new disposable folder with Git installed and configured. Create note.txt containing first. Run git init, git add note.txt, and git commit -m "First note". Change the file to draft without committing.

Run this sequence in that practice folder.

```bash
git status
git diff
git stash push -m "practice draft"
git stash list
git stash show -p "stash@{0}"
git stash apply "stash@{0}"
git diff
git stash list
```

push saves the edits and returns the tracked file to its committed content. apply brings the edits back.
After apply, check that note.txt says draft and that stash list still shows the entry. Applying does not remove the saved stash.
pop tries to apply the edits and removes the stash after a successful apply. For this practice, use apply so you can inspect the recovered work while the saved entry remains.
An ordinary stash push does not include new untracked files by default. Check those files separately before assuming your work is saved.
Applying a stash can cause a conflict with newer edits. The stash is local to this repository; it is not a published commit or remote backup.

before.question: After a successful git stash apply, you verify the recovered file. Is the stash entry automatically removed?
choices: Yes. apply always drops the saved entry immediately.
Yes. apply publishes a remote backup.
No. apply keeps the entry; removing it is a separate action.
before.explanation: apply restores changes without deleting the stash entry. pop has different success behavior.

after.question: After git stash apply succeeds, is the stash entry automatically removed?
choices: Yes. apply publishes it as a backup.
No. apply keeps it; removal is separate.
after.explanation: apply restores the edits while keeping the stash entry.
